items.sentence_raw: In general, it is plausible to suppose that we should prefer peace and quiet to noise.

And yet most of us have had the experience of having to adjust to sleeping in the mountains or the countryside because it was initially 'too quiet', an experience that suggests that humans are capable of adapting to a wide range of noise levels.
items.explain: Q27: The passage says people must *'adjust to sleeping in the mountains'* because it was *'too quiet'*. This means they are used to city noise, so **'adapted to a higher noise level'** matches this idea. ***Option A is a trap*** because the text says we generally *'prefer peace and quiet'*, not that we dislike it. The answer is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: Research supports this view.
For example, Glass and Singer (1972) exposed people to short bursts of very loud noise and then measured their ability to work out problems and their physiological reactions to the noise.
The noise was quite disruptive at first, but after about four minutes the subjects were doing just as well on their tasks as control subjects who were not exposed to noise.
items.explain:
Q28: The text states that after four minutes, subjects were *'doing just as well'* as those without noise. **'Doing just as well'** means the noise did not stop them from solving problems for long. This matches option **C** perfectly. The answer is **C**.

Q35: The text describes Glass and Singer’s study where noise was *'quite disruptive at first'*. This matches the statement about finding it *'difficult at first to concentrate'*. The researcher named in that sentence is **Glass and Singer**. The answer is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: Their physiological arousal also declined quickly to the same levels as those of the control subjects.
But there are limits to adaptation and loud noise becomes more troublesome if the person is required to concentrate on more than one task.

For example, high noise levels interfered with the performance of subjects who were required to monitor three dials at a time, a task not unlike that of an aeroplane pilot or an air-traffic controller (Broadbent, 1957).
items.explain: Q39: The text cites *'Broadbent'* when discussing subjects who had to *'monitor three dials at a time'*. Monitoring three dials is the same as performing **three tasks at the same time**. The answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: Similarly, noise did not affect a subject's ability to track a moving line with a steering wheel, but it did interfere with the subject's ability to repeat numbers while tracking (Finkelman and Glass, 1970).
items.explain:
Q29: The passage says noise *'did not affect'* the ability to *'track a moving line'*. **'Did not affect'** means **'not likely to interfere with'**, and tracking is a **single task**. Options B, C, and D all describe tasks where noise *did* cause problems. So the answer is **A**.

Q40: The passage attributes the finding about repeating numbers while tracking to *'Finkelman and Glass'*. This matches the statement about capacity to *'repeat numbers while carrying out another task'**. The answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: Probably the most significant finding from research on noise is that its predictability is more important than how loud it is.
We are much more able to 'tune out' chronic background noise, even if it is quite loud, than to work under circumstances with unexpected intrusions of noise.
items.explain: Q30: The summary contrasts intense noise with another type that hurts performance more. The passage says *'unexpected intrusions of noise'* are harder to handle than loud background noise. **'Unexpected'** is the exact word needed here to complete the contrast. The answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: In the Glass and Singer study, in which subjects were exposed to bursts of noise as they worked on a task, some subjects heard loud bursts and others heard soft bursts.

For some subjects, the bursts were spaced exactly one minute apart (predictable noise); others heard the same amount of noise overall, but the bursts occurred at random intervals (unpredictable noise).
items.explain: Q31: The text explains that some heard predictable noise while others heard *'the same amount of noise overall'*. This phrase fits the blank to show both groups got equal total noise. The answer is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: Subjects reported finding the predictable and unpredictable noise equally annoying, and all subjects performed at about the same level during the noise portion of the experiment.
items.explain: Q32: The passage states clearly that *'all subjects performed at about the same level'* during the noise. This exact phrase fills the blank to describe their equal performance. The answer is **F**.

items.sentence_raw: But the different noise conditions had quite different after-effects when the subjects were required to proofread written material under conditions of no noise.

As shown in Table 1 the unpredictable noise produced more errors in the later proofreading task than predictable noise; and soft, unpredictable noise actually produced slightly more errors on this task than the loud, predictable noise.
items.explain: Q33: The text says unpredictable noise *'produced more errors'* in the later proofreading task. **'Produced more errors'** means exactly the same as **'made more mistakes than'**. The answer is **I**.

items.sentence_raw: Apparently, unpredictable noise produces more fatigue than predictable noise, but it takes a while for this fatigue to take its toll on performance.
items.explain: Q34: The passage links fatigue to *'unpredictable noise'* specifically. Since the previous sentence mentioned unpredictable noise causing errors, **'unexpected'** fits here as a synonym. The answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: Predictability is not the only variable that reduces or eliminates the negative effects of noise.
Another is control.
If the individual knows that he or she can control the noise, this seems to eliminate both its negative effects at the time and its after-effects.
items.explain: Q37: The text says if a person knows they can *'control the noise'*, negative effects disappear. This matches the idea that problems do not arise if the subject *'knows they can make it stop'**. This finding comes from **Glass and Singer**. The answer is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: This is true even if the individual never actually exercises his or her option to turn the noise off (Glass and Singer, 1972).
Just the knowledge that one has control is sufficient.
The studies discussed so far exposed people to noise for only short periods and only transient effects were studied.
But the major worry about noisy environments is that living day after day with chronic noise may produce serious, lasting effects.

One study, suggesting that this worry is a realistic one, compared elementary school pupils who attended schools near Los Angeles's busiest airport with students who attended schools in quiet neighbourhoods (Cohen et al., 1980).
It was found that children from the noisy schools had higher blood pressure and were more easily distracted than those who attended the quiet schools.
Moreover, there was no evidence of adaptability to the noise.
In fact, the longer the children had attended the noisy schools, the more distractible they became.
The effects also seem to be long lasting.

A follow-up study showed that children who were moved to less noisy classrooms still showed greater distractibility one year later than students who had always been in the quiet schools (Cohen et al, 1981).
items.explain: Q36: The passage mentions a follow-up study by *'Cohen et al'* showing effects lasted *'one year later'*. This directly connects to the statement about changes observed *'a year later'**. The answer is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: It should be noted that the two groups of children had been carefully matched by the investigators so that they were comparable in age, ethnicity, race, and social class.

Since this specific detail is missing, the answer is **None of the above**. Remember, ***NOT GIVEN means the information is absent, not wrong***.
